title: Manage the quality of the harvesting of animal products

lessons.title: What quality means for animal products
lessons.html:
Quality starts on the farm

Animal products such as milk, eggs, wool, mohair, honey and animals sent for slaughter are judged by the buyer long before they reach a shop. A dairy pays on butterfat, protein and bacterial counts. A wool broker grades on fibre diameter, length, strength and contamination. An abattoir pays on carcass grade, bruising and condition. As a supervisor you manage the harvesting so that the farm gets the best price and the product is safe to eat or use.

The main quality factors

  • Hygiene – clean animals, clean equipment, clean hands and clean containers prevent bacterial contamination of milk, eggs and honey.
  • Residues – no milk, eggs or animals may be sold while a medicine or remedy withdrawal period is still running. Always follow the product label and your vet, and record every treatment.
  • Physical damage – bruising from rough handling, cracked eggs, second cuts in wool and stained fleeces all lower value.
  • Foreign material – plastic baling twine in wool, faeces on eggs, flies or hair in milk.
  • Temperature and time – milk must be cooled quickly; eggs must be collected often and kept cool and out of the sun.

Legal and buyer requirements

Products for human consumption fall under food safety rules, and animals for slaughter fall under the Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000. Medicines and stock remedies are controlled by Act 36 of 1947 and must be used according to label. Buyers often add their own standards, for example a milk buyer's penalty scale or a wool buyer's classing standard. Find out exactly what your buyer measures and how they pay, because that tells you where to focus.

Your job is to turn these requirements into simple daily work rules that the team understands and follows, and to check that they are followed.

lessons.title: Planning and supervising the harvest
lessons.html:
Plan before you harvest

Good quality comes from planning. Before shearing, milking, egg collection or loading slaughter stock, the supervisor checks that people, equipment and animals are ready.

A simple pre-harvest checklist

  1. Check treatment records: no animal in a withdrawal period goes into the bulk tank, the egg tray or the truck.
  2. Check equipment: clippers sharpened, milking machine liners and pulsators working, egg trays clean, loading ramp without sharp edges.
  3. Check facilities: shearing shed swept and dry, wool table and bins clean, dairy parlour washed, crates or bakkie clean.
  4. Brief the team: who does what, the hygiene rules, safe handling and what to do with rejects.
  5. Prepare animals: sheep kept dry and off feed for a few hours before shearing; cattle rested and handled calmly before loading.

During the harvest

Walk the line and watch the work. In the shearing shed check for second cuts, skin cuts and that bellies, locks and stained wool are kept separate from the fleece. In the dairy check pre-milking teat preparation and that cups are not left on too long. With slaughter stock check that no sticks or electric prodders are misused and that animals are not overcrowded on the truck. Correct problems at once, kindly and clearly.

Safety

Shearing machines, milking parlours and loading ramps are workplaces under the OHS Act 85 of 1993. Make sure guards are fitted, electrical cords are in good condition, floors are not slippery and nobody stands behind a kicking cow or in a crush with a bull. Never let untrained people use shearing handpieces or work alone with large animals.

lessons.title: Checking, recording and improving quality
lessons.html:
Measure what you produce

You cannot manage quality you do not measure. Use the buyer's results and your own checks to see how the team is doing.

ProductWhat to checkWhere the result comes from
MilkBacterial count, somatic cell count, residues, butterfat, proteinBuyer test slips, own CMT tests
Wool / mohairClass, contamination, yieldBroker or buyer report
EggsCracks, dirty eggs, size gradesPackhouse count, own candling
Slaughter stockGrade, bruising, condemnationsAbattoir kill sheet

Keep records

Record the date, batch, quantity, people on duty, treatments and any problems. Keep the buyer's reports with your records. When a bad result comes back you can then trace it to a day, a group of animals or a person, and fix the cause.

Dealing with problems

When a result is poor, do not just blame the team. Ask what changed: a new worker, a broken machine part, wet weather, a sick animal. Fix the cause, retrain if needed, and check again. Keep rejected product separate and dispose of it correctly, for example milk from treated cows must never go into the bulk tank.

Key points

  • Find out exactly what your buyer measures and pays for.
  • Never harvest from animals still in a withdrawal period; follow the label and your vet.
  • Plan the harvest with a checklist: records, equipment, facilities, team and animals.
  • Supervise during the work and correct problems at once.
  • Record every batch so that poor results can be traced and fixed.
